132248.subject: Zoology
132248.text: Mendelian disorders may be classified based on which of the following?
options: Whether they are dominant or recessive
132248.sol: Broadly, genetic disorders may be grouped into two categories – Mendelian disorders and Chromosomal disorders. Mendelian disorders are mainly determined by alteration or mutation in the single gene. These disorders are transmitted to the offspring on the same lines as we have studied in the principle of inheritance. The pattern of inheritance of such Mendelian disorders can be traced in a family by the pedigree analysis. Most common and prevalent Mendelian disorders are Haemophilia, Cystic fibrosis, Sicklecell anaemia, Colour blindness, Phenylketonuria, Thalassemia, etc. It is important to mention here that such Mendelian disorders may be dominant or recessive. By pedigree analysis one can easily understand whether the trait in question is dominant or recessive. Similarly, the trait may also be linked to the sex chromosome as in case of haemophilia. It is evident that this X-linked recessive trait shows transmission from carrier female to male progeny

132828.sol: One, that all living organisms (species or types) that we see today were created as such. Two, that the diversity was always the same since creation and will be the same in future also. Three, that earth is about 4000 years old. All these ideas were strongly challenged during the nineteenth century. Based on observations made during a sea voyage in a sail ship called H.M.S. Beagle round the world, Charles Darwin concluded that existing living forms share similarities to varying degrees not only among themselves but also with life forms that existed millions of years ago. Many such life forms do not exist any more. There had been extinctions of different life forms in the years gone by just as new forms of life arose at different periods of history of earth. There has been gradual evolution of life forms.

134981.sol: The restriction enzymes and exonuclease both break down nucleic acid chains by cleaving the phosphodiester bond. A phosphodiester bond occurs when exactly two of the hydroxyl groups in phosphoric acid react with hydroxyl groups on other molecules to form two ester bonds. Phosphodiester bonds are central to all life on Earth as they make up the backbone of the strands of nucleic acid.

135085.sol: The above equation describes the exponential or geometric growth pattern of a population (Figure 11.3) and <mark>results in a J-shaped curve when we plot N in relation to time</mark>. If you are familiar with basic calculus, you can derive the integral form of the exponential growth equation asN<sub>t</sub> = N<sub>O</sub> e<sup>rt</sup> whereN<sub>t</sub> = Population density after time tN<sub>O</sub> = Population density at time zeror = intrinsic rate of natural increasee = the base of natural logarithms (2.71828)No population of any species in nature has at its disposal unlimited resources to permit exponential growth. This leads to competition between individuals for limited resources. Eventually, the ‘fittest’ individual will survive and reproduce. The governments of many countries have also realized this fact and introduced various restraints with a view to limit human population growth. In nature, a given habitat has enough resources to support a maximum possible number, beyond which no further growth is possible.

303034.text: Two ideal slits ${S}_{1}$ and ${S}_{2}$ are at~a distance $d$~apart and illuminated by light of wavelength $\lambda$, passing through an ideal source slit $S$, placed on the line through ${S}_{2}$, as shown. The distance between the planes of slits and the source slit is $D$. A screen is held at a distance $D$ from the plane of the slits. The minimum value of $d$ for which there is darkness at $O$& is
303034.sol:
From the above diagram, path difference between the waves reaching at $P$~is,~$\Delta = ( S{S}_{1} - S{S}_{2} ) + \left({S}_{1}O - {S}_{2}O\right)$

From the diagram, we can write,~

$S{S}_{1} - S{S}_{2} = $\sqrt{D^{2} + d^{2}} -$D$

and~${S}_{1}O - {S}_{2}O = $\sqrt{D^{2} + d^{2}} -$D$.

So,

$\Delta $==2\sqrt{D^{2} + d^{2}} -2D = $2D\left($1 + \dfrac{d2}{D2}\right)\dfrac{1}{2} -2D$

From binomial expansion, as~ \left(\dfrac{d}{D}$< 1\right)$,~

$∆ = 2D\left(1 + \dfrac{d2}{2D^{2}}\right) - 2D = \dfrac{d2}{D}$~

To form darkness at $O, ∆$ must be equal to~$\dfrac{λ}{2}$~(minimum value). Then,

$\dfrac{d2}{D} = \dfrac{λ}{2} ⇒ d = \sqrt{\dfrac{\lambdaD}{2}}$

$

303177.chapter: Centre of Mass, Linear momentum, Collision
303177.text: A block of mass $2.0 \text{ kg}$ travelling at $2.0 \text{ m/s}$ undergoes a head-on collision with another block of equal mass kept at rest. If the actual loss in kinetic energy is half of the maximum possible loss, determine the coefficient of restitution.
303177.sol:
The loss in kinetic energy during a head-on collision is given by the formula:

$\Delta K = \dfrac{1}{2} \dfrac{m_1 m_2}{m_1 + m_2} (u_1 - u_2)^2 (1 - e^2)$

Given $m_1 = m_2 = m$ and the second block is at rest ($u_2 = 0$), the loss in kinetic energy becomes:

$\Delta K = \dfrac{1}{2} \dfrac{m \cdot m}{m + m} u_1^2 (1 - e^2) = \dfrac{1}{4} m u_1^2 (1 - e^2)$

The maximum possible loss in kinetic energy occurs when the collision is perfectly inelastic, i.e., $e = 0$:

$\Delta K_{\text\max} = \dfrac{1}{4} m u_1^2$

It is given that the actual loss in kinetic energy is half of the maximum possible loss:

$\Delta K = \dfrac{1}{2} \Delta K_{\text\max}$

Substituting the expressions, we get:

$\dfrac{1}{4} m u_1^2 (1 - e^2) = \dfrac{1}{2} \left( $\dfrac{1}{4}$m u_1^2 \right)$

$1 - e^2 = $\dfrac{1}{2}

$e^2 = $\dfrac{1}{2}

$e = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}$

303499.text: A staircase contains three steps, each $10\text{ cm}$ high and $20 \text{ cm}$ wide, as shown in the figure. Determine the minimum horizontal velocity, in m/s, of a ball rolling off the uppermost plane so that it directly hits the lowest plane.
303499.sol:
Let the edge of the uppermost plane be the origin $(0,0)$.

The staircase has steps of height $h = 10 \text{ cm} = 0.1 \text{ m}$ and width $w = 20 \text{ cm} = 0.2 \text{ m}$.

From the given figure, to directly hit the lowest plane, the ball must clear the edge of the second step.

The coordinates of the edge of the second step are $x = 2w = 0.4 \text{ m}$ and $y = -2h = -0.2 \text{ m}$.

The equation of the trajectory of the ball is given by:

$y = -\dfrac{gx^2}{2u^2}$

For the ball to just clear the second step, its trajectory must pass through the point $(0.4, -0.2)$. Substituting these values into the trajectory equation:

$-0.2 = -\dfrac{10 \times (0.4)^2}{2u^2}$

$0.2 = \dfrac{10 \times 0.16}{2u^2}$

$0.2 = \dfrac{0.8}{u^2}$

$u^2 = \dfrac{0.8}{0.2} = 4$

$u = 2 \text{ m/s}$

Thus, the minimum horizontal velocity required is $2 \text{ m/s}$.

Answer: $2$

303792.text: A parallel beam of light of wavelength $620 \text{ nm}$ is focused by a convex lens of diameter $8.0 \text{ cm}$. Determine the diameter of the central bright spot formed if the light is focused at a distance of $20 \text{ cm}$ from the lens.
303792.sol:
Given:
Wavelength of light, $\lambda = 620 \text{ nm} = 620 \times 10^{-9} \text{ m}$
Diameter of the lens, $D = 8.0 \text{ cm} = 8.0 \times 10^{-2} \text{ m}$
Focal length of the lens, $f = 20 \text{ cm} = 20 \times 10^{-2} \text{ m}$

The radius of the central bright spot (Airy disk) formed by a lens is given by:
$r = \dfrac{1.22 \lambda f}{D}$

The diameter of the central bright spot is:
$d = 2r = \dfrac{2.44 \lambda f}{D}$

Substituting the given values:
$d = \dfrac{2.44 \times 620 \times 10^{-9} \times 20 \times 10^{-2}}{8.0 \times 10^{-2}}$

$d = \dfrac{2.44 \times 620 \times 10^{-9} \times 20}{8.0}$

$d = 2.44 \times 1550 \times 10^{-9} \text{ m}$

$d = 3782 \times 10^{-9} \text{ m}$

$d = 3.782 \times 10^{-6} \text{ m}$

Rounding to two significant figures, we get:
$d \approx 3.8 \times 10^{-6} \text{ m}$

303871.text: A flywheel with a moment of inertia of $5.0 \text{ kg-m}^2$ is rotated at a speed of $60 \text{ rad/s}$. Due to friction at the axle, it comes to rest in $5.0 \text{ minutes}$. Determine the angular momentum of the wheel $1 \text{ minute}$ before it stops rotating.
303871.sol:
Initial angular velocity, $\omega_0 = 60 \text{ rad/s}$

Time taken to come to rest, $t = 5.0 \text{ minutes} = 300 \text{ s}$

Final angular velocity, $\omega = 0$

Using the first equation of rotational motion, $\omega = \omega_0 + \alpha t$

$0 = 60 + \alpha (300)$

$\alpha = -\dfrac{60}{300} = -0.2 \text{ rad/s}^2$

We need to find the angular momentum $1 \text{ minute}$ ($60 \text{ s}$) before it stops. The time elapsed from the start is $t' = 5.0 - 1.0 = 4.0 \text{ minutes} = 240 \text{ s}$.

Angular velocity at $t' = 240 \text{ s}$ is given by:

$\omega' = \omega_0 + \alpha t'$

$\omega' = 60 + (-0.2)(240) = 60 - 48 = 12 \text{ rad/s}$

Angular momentum at this instant is:

$L = I\omega'$

$L = 5.0 \times 12 = 60 \text{ kg-m}^2/\text{s}$

303976.text: A man starts pulling on the cord when the spring is in its unstretched state. The block has a mass of $M$. Given that the man exerts a constant force $F$, determine the kinetic energy of the block at the instant it passes through the equilibrium position.
303976.sol:
The equilibrium position of the block is reached when the net force acting on it is zero. At this position, the constant applied force $F$ is balanced by the restoring force of the spring.

$F = kx_0 \Rightarrow x_0 = \dfrac{F}{k}$

According to the work-energy theorem, the net work done on the block equals its change in kinetic energy:

$W_{\text{net}} = \Delta K$

The work done by the constant force $F$ is:

$W_F = F x_0 = F \left(\dfrac{F}{k}\right) = \dfrac{F^2}{k}$

The work done by the spring force is:

$W_s = -\dfrac{1}{2} k x_0^2 = -\dfrac{1}{2} k \left(\dfrac{F}{k}\right)^2 = -\dfrac{F^2}{2k}$

Since the block starts from rest, its initial kinetic energy is zero. The kinetic energy $K$ at the equilibrium position is:

$K = W_F + W_s = \dfrac{F^2}{k} - \dfrac{F^2}{2k} = \dfrac{F^2}{2k}$

304402.text: Three identical cars, $A$, $B$, and $C$, travel at the same speed across three bridges. Car $A$ drives on a flat bridge, car $B$ on a bridge that is convex upward, and car $C$ on a bridge that is concave upward. Let $F_A$, $F_B$, and $F_C$ denote the normal forces exerted by the cars on the bridges when they are at the center of the bridges. Which of the following statements is correct?
options: $F_B$ is the largest of the three forces
$F_A$ is the largest of the three forces
$F_C$ is the largest of the three forces
304402.sol:
For car $A$ moving on a flat bridge, the vertical acceleration is zero. The normal force is given by $F_A = mg$.

For car $B$ moving on a convex upward bridge, the centripetal acceleration is directed downwards towards the center of curvature. The equation of motion is $mg - F_B = \dfrac{mv^2}{R}$, which gives $F_B = mg - \dfrac{mv^2}{R}$.

For car $C$ moving on a concave upward bridge, the centripetal acceleration is directed upwards towards the center of curvature. The equation of motion is $F_C - mg = \dfrac{mv^2}{R}$, which gives $F_C = mg + \dfrac{mv^2}{R}$.

Comparing the three normal forces, we get $F_C > F_A > F_B$.

Therefore, $F_C$ is the largest of the three forces.

304985.subject: Physics
304985.text: Zero work is performed by a force on an object if
options: the force remains perpendicular to its acceleration at all times
the force remains perpendicular to its velocity at all times
the object moves such that the point of application of the force remains stationary
the object stays stationary while the point of application of the force moves along the object
304985.sol:
The work done by a force on an object is defined as $W = \int \vec{F} \cdot d\vec{r}$, where $d\vec{r}$ is the displacement of the material point of the object at which the force acts.

If the force is perpendicular to the acceleration, it is not necessarily perpendicular to the velocity. For instance, a force acting on a particle moving with a velocity that has components both parallel and perpendicular to the force can still do work, even if the net acceleration is purely perpendicular to the force. Hence, work is not guaranteed to be zero in this case.

If the force remains perpendicular to the velocity at all times, the instantaneous power delivered is $P = \vec{F} \cdot \vec{v} = 0$. Since work is the integral of power over time, the work performed is exactly zero.

If the object moves such that the point of application of the force remains stationary, the displacement of the specific material point where the force acts is zero ($d\vec{r} = 0$). A common example is the normal force exerted by a fixed hinge on a swinging door. Since there is no displacement of the point of application, the work done is zero.

If the object remains strictly stationary, all of its material points are at rest. Even if the spatial point of application of the force moves along the object (for example, kinetic friction acting on a fixed floor when a block slides over it), the displacement of any material point of the object is zero. Thus, $d\vec{r} = 0$ and the mechanical work done on the object is zero.

305819.subject: Physics
305819.text: A gas undergoes a cyclic process $ABCA$ as depicted in the figure. If $2.4 \text{ cal}$ of heat is supplied during this process, what is the value of $J$?
305819.sol:
For a cyclic process, the change in internal energy is zero ($\Delta U = 0$).

According to the first law of thermodynamics, the net heat supplied is equal to the net work done:
$Q = W$

The net work done $W$ is the area enclosed by the cycle on the $P-V$ diagram.

From the given graph, the cycle forms a right-angled triangle with vertices at $A(100 \text{ kPa}, 500 \text{ cc})$, $B(200 \text{ kPa}, 500 \text{ cc})$, and $C(100 \text{ kPa}, 700 \text{ cc})$.

The base of the triangle is $\Delta P = 200 \text{ kPa} - 100 \text{ kPa} = 100 \times 10^3 \text{ Pa}$.

The height of the triangle is $\Delta V = 700 \text{ cc} - 500 \text{ cc} = 200 \times 10^{-6} \text{ m}^3$.

The work done is the area of this triangle:
$W = \dfrac{1}{2} \times \Delta P \times \Delta V$
$W = \dfrac{1}{2} \times (100 \times 10^3) \times (200 \times 10^{-6}) = 10 \text{ J}$

The net heat supplied is given as $Q = 2.4 \text{ cal}$.

Using the relation $W = JQ$, where $J$ is the mechanical equivalent of heat:
$10 = J \times 2.4$
$J = \dfrac{10}{2.4} = \dfrac{100}{24} \approx 4.17 \text{ J/cal}$

Answer: $4.17 \text{ J/cal}$

305920.text: A circular coil with a radius of $2.0 \text{ cm}$ consists of $500$ turns and carries a current of $1.0 \text{ A}$. The axis of the coil forms an angle of $30^{}^{{}^{\circ}}$ with a uniform magnetic field of magnitude $0.40 \text{ T}$ present in the region. Determine the torque acting on the coil.
305920.sol:
Given:
Radius of the coil, $r = 2.0 \text{ cm} = 0.02 \text{ m}$
Number of turns, $N = 500$
Current, $I = 1.0 \text{ A}$
Magnetic field, $B = 0.40 \text{ T}$
Angle between the axis of the coil and the magnetic field, $\theta = 30^{}^{{}^{\circ}}$

The magnetic moment of the coil is given by:
$M = N I A = N I (\pi r^2)$

Substituting the values:
$M = 500 \times 1.0 \times \pi \times (0.02)^2 = 500 \times 0.0004 \pi = 0.2 \pi \text{ A m}^2$

The torque acting on the coil is:
$\tau = M B \sin\theta$

Substituting the values:
$\tau = 0.2 \pi \times 0.40 \times \sin 30^{}^{{}^{\circ}}$
$\tau = 0.08 \pi \times 0.5$
$\tau = 0.04 \pi \text{ N m}$

Using $\pi \approx 3.14$:
$\tau \approx 0.04 \times 3.14 = 0.1256 \text{ N m} \approx 0.13 \text{ N m}$

305973.chapter: Magnetic Field due to a Current
305973.text: A circular loop of radius $r$ carries a current $i$. How must a long, straight wire carrying a current $4i$ be positioned in the plane of the circle such that the magnetic field at the centre becomes zero?
options: At a distance of $\dfrac{4r}{\pi}$ from the centre, with its current direction opposite to that in the nearest part of the loop
At a distance of $\dfrac{2r}{\pi}$ from the centre, with its current direction the same as that in the nearest part of the loop
At a distance of $\dfrac{4r}{\pi}$ from the centre, with its current direction the same as that in the nearest part of the loop
At a distance of $\dfrac{2r}{\pi}$ from the centre, with its current direction opposite to that in the nearest part of the loop
305973.sol:
The magnetic field at the centre of the circular loop due to its own current $i$ is given by:

$B_1 = \dfrac{\mu_0 i}{2r}$

The magnetic field at the centre due to the long straight wire carrying current $4i$ at a distance $d$ is:

$B_2 = \dfrac{\mu_0 (4i)}{2\pi d}$

For the net magnetic field at the centre to be zero, the magnitudes of the magnetic fields must be equal and their directions must be opposite. Equating the magnitudes:

$\dfrac{\mu_0 i}{2r} = \dfrac{\mu_0 (4i)}{2\pi d}$

$d = \dfrac{4r}{\pi}$

For the fields to be opposite at the centre, the straight wire must produce a magnetic field in the opposite direction to that of the loop. By the right-hand thumb rule, if the straight wire is placed near the loop, its current must flow in the direction opposite to the current in the nearest part of the circular loop. This ensures that the magnetic field produced by the straight wire at the centre opposes the magnetic field produced by the loop.

306336.text: A servo voltage stabiliser limits its output voltage to $220 \text{ V} \pm 1\%$. When an electric bulb rated at $220 \text{ V}$, $100 \text{ W}$ is connected to this stabiliser, determine the minimum and maximum power consumed by the bulb.
306336.sol:
The power consumed by the bulb is given by $P = \dfrac{V^2}{R}$.

For small variations, the fractional change in power is:

$\dfrac{\Delta P}{P} = 2 \dfrac{\Delta V}{V}$

Given that the voltage variation is $\pm 1\%$, we have:

$\dfrac{\Delta P}{P} = \pm 2(1\%) = \pm 2\%$

The nominal power of the bulb is $P = 100 \text{ W}$.

The variation in power is $\Delta P = \pm 2\%$ of $100 \text{ W} = \pm 2 \text{ W}$.

306572.subject: Physics
306572.text: A tangent galvanometer is directly connected to an ideal battery. If the coil's number of turns is doubled, the deflection will
306572.sol:
The magnetic field at the center of the coil of a tangent galvanometer is given by $B = \dfrac{\mu_0 N I}{2r}$.

The current through the coil is $I = \dfrac{V}{R}$, where $V$ is the voltage of the ideal battery and $R$ is the resistance of the coil.

The resistance of the coil is proportional to the total length of the wire, which is proportional to the number of turns $N$ (assuming the radius $r$ of the coil is constant). Let $R = c N$, where $c$ is a constant.

Substituting $I$ in the expression for $B$, we get:

$B = \dfrac{\mu_0 N}{2r} \left( \dfrac{V}{c N} \right) = \dfrac{\mu_0 V}{2 r c}$

This shows that the magnetic field $B$ is independent of the number of turns $N$.

The deflection $\theta$ in a tangent galvanometer is given by $B = B_H \tan \theta$, where $B_H$ is the horizontal component of the Earth's magnetic field.

Since $B$ remains unchanged, the deflection $\theta$ will also remain unchanged.

306792.subject: Physics
306792.text: For measuring the magnetic moment of a bar magnet, one could use
options: an oscillation magnetometer, provided the earth's horizontal field is known
a deflection galvanometer, provided the earth's horizontal field is known
both deflection and oscillation magnetometer, if the earth's horizontal field is not known
306792.sol:
The time period of oscillation of a bar magnet in an oscillation magnetometer is given by $T = 2\pi \sqrt{\dfrac{I}{MB_H}}$. This gives the product $MB_H = \dfrac{4\pi^2 I}{T^2}$. If the earth's horizontal magnetic field $B_H$ and the moment of inertia $I$ are known, the magnetic moment $M$ can be determined.

In a deflection magnetometer, the deflection $\theta$ is related to $M$ and $B_H$ by $\dfrac{M}{B_H} = k \tan\theta$, where $k$ is a constant depending on the position (Tan A or Tan B). If $B_H$ is known, $M$ can be determined.

If $B_H$ is not known, we can use both instruments. The oscillation magnetometer gives the product $MB_H$, and the deflection magnetometer gives the ratio $\dfrac{M}{B_H}$. Multiplying these two quantities yields $M^2$, allowing us to find $M$ without knowing $B_H$.

A tangent galvanometer is primarily used to measure electric current, not the magnetic moment of a bar magnet.

309601.subject: Chemistry
309601.text: Which of the following represents the most stable canonical structure of the given molecule?
309601.sol:
To determine the most stable canonical structure, we need to look for the structure that maximizes aromaticity in the rings.

In the given molecule, the exocyclic double bond connects a six-membered pyran-like ring and a five-membered cyclopentadiene-like ring. We can draw resonance structures by heterolytically cleaving this double bond.

If the $\pi$ electrons of the exocyclic double bond are shifted towards the five-membered ring, the connecting carbon of the five-membered ring gains a negative charge. This forms a cyclopentadienyl anion. The cyclopentadienyl anion has $6\pi$ electrons ($2$ from each of the two double bonds and $2$ from the lone pair/negative charge), making it aromatic according to Hückel's rule ($4n+2\pi$ electrons, with $n=1$).

Simultaneously, the connecting carbon of the six-membered ring acquires a positive charge. The adjacent oxygen atom has lone pairs and can donate one to form a double bond with this positively charged carbon. This places a formal positive charge on the oxygen atom and results in a pyrylium cation structure for the six-membered ring. The pyrylium cation has $3$ double bonds within the ring, giving it $6\pi$ electrons, which makes it aromatic as well.

The resulting canonical structure consists of two aromatic rings: a pyrylium cation and a cyclopentadienyl anion. Because both rings are aromatic, this zwitterionic structure is highly stable.

Looking at the given options, Option (A) exactly represents this doubly aromatic structure, with a negative charge on the five-membered ring and a positive charge on the oxygen atom of the six-membered ring, along with the correct placement of double bonds.

Other options are less stable; for instance, Option (B) would result in a cyclopentadienyl cation, which has $4\pi$ electrons and is anti-aromatic and highly unstable.

6a13e468688ac6d0667aad62.subject: Biology
6a13e468688ac6d0667aad62.text: To fix 5 molecules of $CO_2$ during the Calvin cycle, what is the total number of ATP and NADPH molecules consumed respectively?
6a13e468688ac6d0667aad62.sol:
In the Calvin cycle, the fixation of one molecule of $CO_2$ requires $3$ molecules of ATP and $2$ molecules of NADPH.

For the fixation of $5$ molecules of $CO_2$, the total number of ATP molecules consumed is $5 \times 3 = 15$ ATP.

The total number of NADPH molecules consumed is $5 \times 2 = 10$ NADPH.

Thus, $15$ ATP and $10$ NADPH molecules are consumed.

Answer: 15 ATP and 10 NADPH

6a16f3287cfacf7984f86725.subject: Biology
6a16f3287cfacf7984f86725.text: The given figure represents the longitudinal section of a drupe fruit. Identify the layer marked as 'Y'.
6a16f3287cfacf7984f86725.sol:
The given figure represents the longitudinal section of a mango, which is a drupe fruit.

In drupe fruits, the pericarp is well differentiated into three distinct layers:
1. Epicarp: The outer thin skin (exocarp).
2. Mesocarp: The middle fleshy, edible part.
3. Endocarp: The inner hard and stony layer.

The label 'Y' points to the middle fleshy layer of the fruit. Therefore, 'Y' represents the mesocarp.

Answer: Mesocarp

6a2a77bdfad2360f42564bb4.text:
Given below is an image containing four chemical structures labeled A, B, C, and D, which act as intermediates in the preparation of phenol.

Match the structures in List I with their corresponding formation reactions in List II :

List IList II
AStructure A1Intermediate formed when chlorobenzene is fused with NaOH at $623\text{ K}$
BStructure B2Formed by aerial oxidation of isopropylbenzene
CStructure C3Formed by treating aniline with nitrous acid at $273-278\text{ K}$
DStructure D4Formed by electrophilic substitution of benzene with oleum


Choose the correct answer from the options given below :
6a2a77bdfad2360f42564bb4.sol:
Structure A is cumene hydroperoxide, which is formed by the aerial oxidation of cumene (isopropylbenzene). Thus, A matches with 2.

Structure B is benzenediazonium chloride, which is formed by the diazotization of aniline using nitrous acid at $273-278\text{ K}$. Thus, B matches with 3.

Structure C is sodium phenoxide, which is an intermediate in Dow's process, formed when chlorobenzene is fused with NaOH at $623\text{ K}$ and $300\text{ atm}$. Thus, C matches with 1.

Structure D is benzenesulfonic acid, which is formed by the sulfonation of benzene using oleum. Thus, D matches with 4.

The correct matching is A-2, B-3, C-1, D-4.

Answer: A-2, B-3, C-1, D-4

Given below are two statements:

Statement I : The synthetic auxin 2,4-D is widely used to prepare weed-free lawns by selectively killing mature monocotyledonous weeds.
Statement II : Auxins control xylem differentiation and help in cell division.

In the light of the above statements, choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below:
options: Both Statement I and Statement II are incorrect
Both Statement I and Statement II are correct
Statement I is incorrect but Statement II is correct
Statement I is correct but Statement II is incorrect
6a104ffb8b46719ce7976d30.sol:
Statement I is incorrect because the synthetic auxin 2,4-D is widely used to kill dicotyledonous weeds, not monocotyledonous weeds. It does not affect mature monocotyledonous plants and is used by gardeners to prepare weed-free lawns.

Statement II is correct as auxins are known to control xylem differentiation and help in cell division.

Therefore, Statement I is incorrect but Statement II is correct.

Answer: Statement I is incorrect but Statement II is correct

6a2109b2219e1ae5a1722998.text: Which of the following statements correctly describes the distribution and function of photosystems in the chloroplast?
options: Grana lamellae possess only Photosystem II, which is responsible for the synthesis of both ATP and NADPH.
Stroma lamellae lack Photosystem II but contain NADP reductase, allowing them to perform cyclic photophosphorylation.
Cyclic photophosphorylation usually occurs when only light of wavelengths beyond $680\text{ nm}$ are available for excitation.
Non-cyclic photophosphorylation is restricted to stroma lamellae and requires the presence of both PS I and PS II.
6a2109b2219e1ae5a1722998.sol:
Grana lamellae have both PS I and PS II, whereas stroma lamellae lack PS II and NADP reductase enzyme.

Stroma lamellae contain only PS I and perform cyclic photophosphorylation, which synthesizes ATP but not NADPH.

Cyclic photophosphorylation occurs when only light of wavelengths beyond $680\text{ nm}$ is available for excitation, as PS II (which absorbs at $680\text{ nm}$) is not activated, leaving only PS I (which absorbs at $700\text{ nm}$) functional.

Non-cyclic photophosphorylation occurs in grana lamellae where both PS I and PS II are present.

Answer: Cyclic photophosphorylation usually occurs when only light of wavelengths beyond $680\text{ nm}$ are available for excitation.

6a7a1ff8997c4f00dd03384b.subject: Physics
6a7a1ff8997c4f00dd03384b.text:
A student measures the resistance, diameter, and length of a wire to determine its electrical resistivity. The measured values are:
Resistance, $R = (10.0 \pm 0.1) \,\Omega$
Diameter, $d = (2.00 \pm 0.02) \text{ mm}$
Length, $l = (50.0 \pm 0.5) \text{ cm}$

The maximum percentage error in the calculated value of resistivity is:
6a7a1ff8997c4f00dd03384b.sol:
The formula for the electrical resistivity $\rho$ of a wire is given by:
$\rho = \dfrac{R A}{l} = \dfrac{R (\pi d^2 / 4)}{l}$

The maximum fractional error in resistivity is the sum of the fractional errors of the individual quantities (with the power of $d$ bringing a factor of 2):
$\dfrac{\Delta \rho}{\rho} = \dfrac{\Delta R}{R} + 2\dfrac{\Delta d}{d} + \dfrac{\Delta l}{l}$

Calculating the individual percentage errors:
Percentage error in $R = \left(\dfrac{0.1}{10.0}\right) \times 100 = 1\%$
Percentage error in $d = \left(\dfrac{0.02}{2.00}\right) \times 100 = 1\%$
Percentage error in $l = \left(\dfrac{0.5}{50.0}\right) \times 100 = 1\%$

Substituting these into the error equation:
Maximum percentage error in $\rho = 1\% + 2(1\%) + 1\% = 4\%$

Answer: 4

6a7a1ff820c5901923d87bd4.subject: Physics
6a7a1ff820c5901923d87bd4.text: A player can throw a ball vertically upwards to a maximum height of $20\text{ m}$. What is the maximum horizontal distance the player can throw the same ball?
6a7a1ff820c5901923d87bd4.sol:
The maximum vertical height a person can throw a ball is achieved when the ball is thrown vertically upwards ($\theta = 90^\circ$).

$H_{\max} = \dfrac{u^2}{2g} = 20\text{ m}$

$\Rightarrow \dfrac{u^2}{g} = 40\text{ m}$

The maximum horizontal range is achieved when the ball is thrown at an angle of $45^\circ$.

$R_{\max} = \dfrac{u^2}{g}$

Substituting the value of $\dfrac{u^2}{g}$, we get:

$R_{\max} = 40\text{ m}$

Answer: $40\text{ m}$

6a7a1ff8611f0968b04417c8.text:
A block of mass $2\text{ kg}$ is sliding on a rough horizontal surface. The velocity-time graph of the block's motion is a straight line. The graph intersects the velocity axis at $12\text{ m s}^{-1}$ and the time axis at $4\text{ s}$. The value of the coefficient of kinetic friction between the block and the surface is:
(Take $g = 10\text{ m s}^{-2}$)
6a7a1ff8611f0968b04417c8.sol:
From the velocity-time graph, the initial velocity is $u = 12\text{ m s}^{-1}$ and the final velocity is $v = 0$ at $t = 4\text{ s}$.

The magnitude of deceleration is given by the slope of the velocity-time graph:
$a = \dfrac{12 - 0}{4} = 3\text{ m s}^{-2}$

The only horizontal force acting on the block is the kinetic friction, which provides the deceleration.
$f_k = m a$
$\mu_k m g = m a$
$\mu_k = \dfrac{a}{g}$

Substituting the values:
$\mu_k = \dfrac{3}{10} = 0.3$

Answer: $0.3$

6a7a1ff88531018819c27ba5.text: Two solid discs, A and B, are made of the same material. Disc A has radius $R$ and thickness $t$. Disc B has radius $3R$ and thickness $\dfrac{t}{3}$. Identical constant tangential forces $F$ are applied to the rim of each disc, causing them to rotate about their respective central axes. If the ratio of the angular acceleration of disc A to that of disc B is $x$, then the value of $x$ is ____.
6a7a1ff88531018819c27ba5.sol:
Let the density of the material be $\rho$.

The moment of inertia of a solid disc is $I = \dfrac{1}{2}MR^2 = \dfrac{1}{2}(\rho \pi R^2 t)R^2 = \dfrac{1}{2}\rho \pi R^4 t$.
For disc A: $I_A = \dfrac{1}{2}\rho \pi R^4 t$
For disc B: $I_B = \dfrac{1}{2}\rho \pi (3R)^4 \left(\dfrac{t}{3}\right) = \dfrac{1}{2}\rho \pi (81R^4)\left(\dfrac{t}{3}\right) = 27 \left(\dfrac{1}{2}\rho \pi R^4 t\right) = 27 I_A$

The torque produced by the tangential force $F$ is $\tau = F \times \text{radius}$.
For disc A: $\tau_A = F R$
For disc B: $\tau_B = F (3R) = 3 \tau_A$

Using Newton's second law for rotation, $\alpha = \dfrac{\tau}{I}$:
For disc A: $\alpha_A = \dfrac{\tau_A}{I_A}$
For disc B: $\alpha_B = \dfrac{\tau_B}{I_B} = \dfrac{3 \tau_A}{27 I_A} = \dfrac{1}{9} \alpha_A$

The ratio of their angular accelerations is:
$\dfrac{\alpha_A}{\alpha_B} = 9$

Thus, $x = 9$.

Answer: $9$

6a7a1ff84b6eb4a10cc2e6c2.sol:
The relationship between velocity $v$ and displacement $x$ for a particle in simple harmonic motion is:

$\dfrac{x^2}{A^2} + \dfrac{v^2}{(A\omega)^2} = 1$

This is the equation of an ellipse with semi-axes $A$ and $A\omega$. The area $S$ of this ellipse is given by:

$S = \pi (A)(A\omega)$

Since the maximum velocity is $v_0 = A\omega$, we can write the area as:

$S = \pi A v_0$

From this, the amplitude $A$ is:

$A = \dfrac{S}{\pi v_0}$

The maximum acceleration $a_0$ of the particle is given by $a_0 = \omega^2 A$. We can rewrite this in terms of $v_0$ and $A$:

$a_0 = \dfrac{(A\omega)^2}{A} = \dfrac{v_0^2}{A}$

Substituting the expression for $A$:

$a_0 = \dfrac{v_0^2}{\left(\dfrac{S}{\pi v_0}\right)} = \dfrac{\pi v_0^3}{S}$

Answer: $\dfrac{\pi v_0^3}{S}$

6a7a1ff8a0a129de8d3c06ac.subject: Physics
6a7a1ff8a0a129de8d3c06ac.text: A steady current $I$ flows through a wire in the $xy$-plane consisting of three parts: a semi-infinite straight section parallel to the $x$-axis coming from $x = -\infty$ to $x = 0$ at $y = R$, a quarter-circular arc of radius $R$ centered at the origin from $(0, R)$ to $(R, 0)$, and another semi-infinite straight section parallel to the $y$-axis going from $y = 0$ to $y = -\infty$ at $x = R$. The magnitude of the net magnetic field at the origin $(0,0)$ is:
6a7a1ff8a0a129de8d3c06ac.sol:
The wire consists of three segments, and we calculate the magnetic field contribution of each at the origin $(0,0)$.

Segment 1: The semi-infinite straight wire from $x = -\infty$ to $x = 0$ at $y = R$. The perpendicular distance to the origin is $R$. The magnetic field at the origin is $B_1 = \dfrac{\mu_0 I}{4\pi R}$. By the right-hand rule, its direction is into the plane of the paper ($-\hat{k}$).

Segment 2: The quarter-circular arc from $(0, R)$ to $(R, 0)$. The magnetic field at the center of a full circle is $\dfrac{\mu_0 I}{2R}$, so for a quarter circle it is $B_2 = \dfrac{1}{4} \left( \dfrac{\mu_0 I}{2R} \right) = \dfrac{\mu_0 I}{8R}$. The current flows clockwise, so its direction is also into the plane of the paper ($-\hat{k}$).

Segment 3: The semi-infinite straight wire from $y = 0$ to $y = -\infty$ at $x = R$. The perpendicular distance to the origin is $R$. The magnetic field at the origin is $B_3 = \dfrac{\mu_0 I}{4\pi R}$. By the right-hand rule, its direction is into the plane of the paper ($-\hat{k}$).

Since all three contributions point in the same direction, the net magnetic field magnitude is the sum of their magnitudes:
$B = B_1 + B_2 + B_3 = \dfrac{\mu_0 I}{4\pi R} + \dfrac{\mu_0 I}{8R} + \dfrac{\mu_0 I}{4\pi R}$
$B = \dfrac{\mu_0 I}{2\pi R} + \dfrac{\mu_0 I}{8R} = \dfrac{\mu_0 I}{8\pi R} (4 + \pi)$

Answer: $\dfrac{\mu_0 I}{8\pi R} (4 + \pi)$

6a7a1ff86ced61aa3ad47739.text: A sample of hydrogen-like atoms in a specific excited state emits exactly $3$ distinct spectral lines. If the longest and shortest wavelengths among these lines are $\lambda_L$ and $\lambda_S$ respectively, the wavelength of the third spectral line is
6a7a1ff86ced61aa3ad47739.sol:
The number of distinct spectral lines emitted by a sample of atoms in the $n^{\text{th}}$ state is given by $\dfrac{n(n-1)}{2}$.

Given that $3$ lines are emitted, $\dfrac{n(n-1)}{2} = 3 \Rightarrow n = 3$.

The possible transitions are from $n=3$ to $n=1$, $n=3$ to $n=2$, and $n=2$ to $n=1$.

The energy of a transition is inversely proportional to its wavelength ($E = \dfrac{hc}{\lambda}$).

The transition with the maximum energy ($n=3$ to $n=1$) will have the shortest wavelength, so $\lambda_{31} = \lambda_S$.

The transition with the minimum energy ($n=3$ to $n=2$) will have the longest wavelength, so $\lambda_{32} = \lambda_L$.

The third line corresponds to the transition from $n=2$ to $n=1$, let its wavelength be $\lambda_3$.

From energy conservation, the energy of the direct transition is the sum of the energies of the intermediate transitions:
$E_{31} = E_{32} + E_{21}$

$\Rightarrow \dfrac{hc}{\lambda_S} = \dfrac{hc}{\lambda_L} + \dfrac{hc}{\lambda_3}$

$\Rightarrow \dfrac{1}{\lambda_3} = \dfrac{1}{\lambda_S} - \dfrac{1}{\lambda_L} = \dfrac{\lambda_L - \lambda_S}{\lambda_L \lambda_S}$

$\Rightarrow \lambda_3 = \dfrac{\lambda_L \lambda_S}{\lambda_L - \lambda_S}$

Answer: $\dfrac{\lambda_L \lambda_S}{\lambda_L - \lambda_S}$

6a7a1ff81548781841f9c792.subject: Chemistry
6a7a1ff81548781841f9c792.text: A sample of $\text{He}^+$ ions in the ground state is irradiated with monochromatic photons of energy $51.0\text{ eV}$. The maximum number of spectral lines emitted when these ions subsequently de-excite to the ground state is
6a7a1ff81548781841f9c792.sol:
The energy of an electron in a hydrogen-like species is given by $E_n = -13.6 \times \dfrac{Z^2}{n^2} \text{ eV}$.

For the ground state of $\text{He}^+$ ($Z = 2, n = 1$), the energy is:
$E_1 = -13.6 \times \dfrac{2^2}{1^2} = -54.4 \text{ eV}$

When the ions absorb a photon of energy $51.0 \text{ eV}$, the energy of the excited state becomes:
$E_n = -54.4 + 51.0 = -3.4 \text{ eV}$

Using the energy formula to find the principal quantum number $n$ of the excited state:
$-3.4 = -13.6 \times \dfrac{2^2}{n^2}$

$-3.4 = -\dfrac{54.4}{n^2}$

$n^2 = \dfrac{54.4}{3.4} = 16 \Rightarrow n = 4$

The maximum number of spectral lines emitted when the ions de-excite from $n = 4$ to the ground state ($n = 1$) is:
$\text{Number of lines} = \dfrac{n(n - 1)}{2} = \dfrac{4 \times (4 - 1)}{2} = \dfrac{12}{2} = 6$.

Answer: $6$

6a7a1ff8f1474ac34b30f101.subject: Chemistry
6a7a1ff8f1474ac34b30f101.text: Which of the following statements comparing the properties of two chemical species is correct?
options: $[\mathrm{NiCl}_{4}]^{2-}$ and $[\mathrm{PtCl}_{4}]^{2-}$ are isostructural and both are paramagnetic.
$\mathrm{NO}_{2}$ and $\mathrm{BF}_{3}$ are both planar species that possess an incomplete octet around their central atoms.
$\mathrm{SF}_{4}$ and $\mathrm{XeF}_{4}$ both possess expanded octets and the same number of lone pairs on their central atoms.
$\mathrm{NH}_{4}^{+}$ and $\mathrm{AlCl}_{3}$ (monomer) both have complete octets and are tetrahedral.
6a7a1ff8f1474ac34b30f101.sol:
Let us evaluate each statement:

Option 1: $[\mathrm{NiCl}_{4}]^{2-}$ contains $\mathrm{Ni}^{2+}$ (3d$^8$) with weak field $\mathrm{Cl}^{-}$ ligands, resulting in $sp^3$ hybridization (tetrahedral) and 2 unpaired electrons (paramagnetic). $[\mathrm{PtCl}_{4}]^{2-}$ contains $\mathrm{Pt}^{2+}$ (5d$^8$). Since it is a 5d metal, it forms a low-spin $dsp^2$ complex (square planar) and is diamagnetic. They are neither isostructural nor both paramagnetic.

Option 2: $\mathrm{NO}_{2}$ is a bent molecule (which is planar as it has only 3 atoms) with 7 valence electrons around nitrogen (incomplete octet). $\mathrm{BF}_{3}$ is trigonal planar with 6 valence electrons around boron (incomplete octet). This statement is correct.

Option 3: Both $\mathrm{SF}_{4}$ and $\mathrm{XeF}_{4}$ have expanded octets. However, $\mathrm{SF}_{4}$ has 4 bond pairs and 1 lone pair on sulfur, while $\mathrm{XeF}_{4}$ has 4 bond pairs and 2 lone pairs on xenon. They do not have the same number of lone pairs.

Option 4: $\mathrm{NH}_{4}^{+}$ is tetrahedral with a complete octet (8 electrons around N). However, monomeric $\mathrm{AlCl}_{3}$ is trigonal planar ($sp^2$) with an incomplete octet (6 electrons around Al).

Answer: $\mathrm{NO}_{2}$ and $\mathrm{BF}_{3}$ are both planar species that possess an incomplete octet around their central atoms.

6a7a1ff88834bdfd6c191c48.subject: Chemistry
6a7a1ff88834bdfd6c191c48.text:
The standard enthalpy of combustion of methane ($\text{CH}_4$) at $300\text{ K}$ is $-895\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$. When $3.2\text{ g}$ of methane is burnt in a bomb calorimeter at $300\text{ K}$, the temperature of the calorimeter system increases by $4\text{ K}$. The heat capacity of the calorimeter system is ________ $\text{J K}^{-1}$. (Nearest integer)

[Given: $R = 8.3\text{ J K}^{-1}\text{ mol}^{-1}$, molar mass of $\text{C}$ and $\text{H}$ are $12$ and $1\text{ g mol}^{-1}$ respectively. Assume ideal gas behaviour.]
6a7a1ff88834bdfd6c191c48.sol:
The combustion reaction of methane is:
$\text{CH}_4(\text{g}) + 2\text{O}_2(\text{g}) \rightarrow \text{CO}_2(\text{g}) + 2\text{H}_2\text{O}(\text{l})$

The change in the number of gaseous moles is:
$\Delta n_g = 1 - (1 + 2) = -2$

The relationship between enthalpy change ($\Delta H$) and internal energy change ($\Delta U$) is:
$\Delta H = \Delta U + \Delta n_g RT$

Substituting the given values:
$-895 = \Delta U + \dfrac{-2 \times 8.3 \times 300}{1000}$
$-895 = \Delta U - 4.98$
$\Delta U = -890.02\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$

The molar mass of $\text{CH}_4$ is $16\text{ g mol}^{-1}$.
Moles of methane burnt $= \dfrac{3.2}{16} = 0.2\text{ mol}$

The heat released at constant volume ($q_v$) for $0.2\text{ mol}$ is:
$q_v = 0.2 \times 890.02 = 178.004\text{ kJ} = 178004\text{ J}$

The heat capacity of the calorimeter system ($C_v$) is:
$C_v = \dfrac{q_v}{\Delta T} = \dfrac{178004}{4} = 44501\text{ J K}^{-1}$

Answer: $44501$

6a7a1ff8db76c5a7d6152a54.subject: Chemistry
6a7a1ff8db76c5a7d6152a54.text:
Two gaseous reactions have the following rate constants:
$\mathrm{X} \rightarrow \mathrm{Y} \quad k_{1} = 10^{8} e^{\dfrac{-15000}{\mathrm{T}}}$
$\mathrm{P} \rightarrow \mathrm{Q} \quad k_{2} = 10^{6} e^{\dfrac{-x}{\mathrm{T}}}$
If the rate constants of these two reactions become equal at a temperature of $1000$ K, the value of $x$ is $\_\_\_\_$.
(Given: $\ln 10 = 2.3$)
6a7a1ff8db76c5a7d6152a54.sol:
Given that $k_{1} = k_{2}$ at $\mathrm{T} = 1000$ K, we can equate the two expressions:

$10^{8} e^{\dfrac{-15000}{1000}} = 10^{6} e^{\dfrac{-x}{1000}}$

Dividing both sides by $10^{6}$ gives:

$10^{2} e^{-15} = e^{\dfrac{-x}{1000}}$

Dividing both sides by $e^{-15}$ gives:

$10^{2} = e^{\dfrac{15000 - x}{1000}}$

Taking the natural logarithm on both sides:

$\ln(10^{2}) = \dfrac{15000 - x}{1000}$

$2 \ln 10 = \dfrac{15000 - x}{1000}$

Substituting the given value of $\ln 10 = 2.3$:

$2 \times 2.3 = \dfrac{15000 - x}{1000}$

$4.6 = \dfrac{15000 - x}{1000}$

$4600 = 15000 - x$

$x = 15000 - 4600 = 10400$

Answer: $10400$

6a7a1ff8ea89c1d209223d31.text: An oxide of chlorine is known to be a highly reactive oxidizing agent that tends to explode. The oxidation state of chlorine in this specific oxide is $+4$. Identify the chemical formula of this oxide and its primary industrial application.
options: $\text{ClO}_2$, used as a bleaching agent for paper pulp
$\text{Cl}_2\text{O}$, used as a bleaching agent for paper pulp
$\text{ClO}_2$, used primarily as a dehydrating agent
$\text{Cl}_2\text{O}_7$, used as a bleaching agent for paper pulp
6a7a1ff8ea89c1d209223d31.sol:
Let the oxidation state of chlorine in the oxide be $+4$. The formula of the oxide is $\text{ClO}_2$.

Chlorine oxides are generally highly reactive oxidizing agents and tend to explode. Among them, $\text{ClO}_2$ is widely used as a bleaching agent for paper pulp and textiles, and in water treatment.

$\text{Cl}_2\text{O}$ has chlorine in the $+1$ oxidation state, and $\text{Cl}_2\text{O}_7$ has chlorine in the $+7$ oxidation state. Dehydration is not the primary industrial application of $\text{ClO}_2$.

Answer: $\text{ClO}_2$, used as a bleaching agent for paper pulp

6a7a1ff84d7a26204f4765fc.subject: Chemistry
6a7a1ff84d7a26204f4765fc.text: A metal 'M' belonging to the first transition series exhibits the maximum number of oxidation states. It forms three oxides, denoted as X, Y, and Z, where the metal 'M' is in $+2$, $+4$, and $+7$ oxidation states respectively. The acid-base nature of the oxides X, Y, and Z respectively is :
6a7a1ff84d7a26204f4765fc.sol:
The metal in the 3d transition series that exhibits the maximum number of oxidation states (from $+2$ to $+7$) is Manganese (Mn).

The oxides formed are $\mathrm{MnO}$ (oxide X, $+2$ state), $\mathrm{MnO}_2$ (oxide Y, $+4$ state), and $\mathrm{Mn}_2\mathrm{O}_7$ (oxide Z, $+7$ state).

For a given transition metal, the acidic character of its oxides increases with an increase in the oxidation state. Lower oxidation state oxides are basic, intermediate ones are amphoteric, and the highest oxidation state oxides are acidic.

Therefore, $\mathrm{MnO}$ is basic, $\mathrm{MnO}_2$ is amphoteric, and $\mathrm{Mn}_2\mathrm{O}_7$ is acidic.

Answer: Basic, Amphoteric, Acidic

6a7a1ff89fbfb760dde538cb.subject: Chemistry
6a7a1ff89fbfb760dde538cb.text: Which of the following statements regarding the structure of proteins is incorrect?
options: In the $\alpha$-helix structure, the polypeptide chain is stabilized by intermolecular hydrogen bonding.
In the $\beta$-pleated sheet structure, adjacent polypeptide chains are held together by intermolecular hydrogen bonds.
The secondary structure of a protein arises due to the regular folding of the backbone of the polypeptide chain.
The primary structure of a protein refers to the specific sequence in which amino acids are linked together.
6a7a1ff89fbfb760dde538cb.sol:
Let us evaluate each statement:

Statement 1 is incorrect. In the $\alpha$-helix structure, the polypeptide chain twists into a right-handed screw, and the structure is stabilized by intramolecular hydrogen bonding between the $-\text{C=O}$ of one amino acid residue and the $-\text{NH}-$ group of the fourth amino acid residue along the same chain.

Statement 2 is correct. In the $\beta$-pleated sheet structure, all peptide chains are stretched out to nearly maximum extension and then laid side by side, held together by intermolecular hydrogen bonds.

Statement 3 is correct. Secondary structures ($\alpha$-helix and $\beta$-pleated sheet) arise due to the regular folding of the polypeptide backbone.

Statement 4 is correct. The primary structure is defined as the specific sequence of amino acids in the polypeptide chain.

Answer: In the $\alpha$-helix structure, the polypeptide chain is stabilized by intermolecular hydrogen bonding.

6a7a1ff851259af5c65888ec.text: Let $K$ be the sum of the coefficients of the even powers of $x$ in the expansion of $(1+x)^{2N}$. Let $a$ be the middle term in the expansion of $\left(2x + \dfrac{1}{x}\right)^{2N}$. If $\dfrac{^{2N}C_{N-1} K}{a} = \dfrac{25}{13} \times 2^{23}$, then the value of $N$ is equal to:
6a7a1ff851259af5c65888ec.sol:
The sum of the coefficients of the even powers of $x$ in the expansion of $(1+x)^{2N}$ is given by $K = 2^{2N-1}$.

The middle term in the expansion of $\left(2x + \dfrac{1}{x}\right)^{2N}$ is the $(N+1)^{\text{th}}$ term, given by:

$a = \, ^{2N}C_{N} (2x)^N \left(\dfrac{1}{x}\right)^N = \, ^{2N}C_{N} 2^N$

Substitute $K$ and $a$ into the given expression:

$\dfrac{^{2N}C_{N-1} K}{a} = \dfrac{^{2N}C_{N-1} \times 2^{2N-1}}{^{2N}C_{N} \times 2^N}$

Using the property $\dfrac{^{n}C_{r-1}}{^{n}C_{r}} = \dfrac{r}{n-r+1}$, we have $\dfrac{^{2N}C_{N-1}}{^{2N}C_{N}} = \dfrac{N}{2N - (N-1)} = \dfrac{N}{N+1}$.

Thus, the ratio simplifies to:

$\dfrac{N}{N+1} \times 2^{N-1}$

We are given that this ratio is equal to $\dfrac{25}{13} \times 2^{23}$.

Rewrite the given value to match the form of our simplified expression:

$\dfrac{25}{13} \times 2^{23} = \dfrac{25}{26} \times 2^{24}$

Comparing $\dfrac{N}{N+1} \times 2^{N-1}$ with $\dfrac{25}{25+1} \times 2^{25-1}$, we can clearly see that $N = 25$.

Answer: $25$

6a7a1ff857c7872d89929a52.text: Two sides of a triangle lie on the lines $2x - y = 0$ and $x + y = 3$. If the centroid of the triangle is $\left(\dfrac{8}{3}, \dfrac{7}{3}\right)$, then the equation of the third side is
6a7a1ff857c7872d89929a52.sol:
Let the vertices of the triangle be $A$, $B$, and $C$.

The coordinates of vertex $A$ can be found by solving the equations of the given sides $2x - y = 0$ and $x + y = 3$.
Substituting $y = 2x$ into the second equation gives $x + 2x = 3 \Rightarrow x = 1$.
Thus, $y = 2$, and the vertex is $A(1, 2)$.

Let $M(x_m, y_m)$ be the midpoint of the third side $BC$. The centroid $G\left(\dfrac{8}{3}, \dfrac{7}{3}\right)$ divides the median $AM$ in the ratio $2:1$.
Using the section formula:
$x_G = \dfrac{2x_m + x_A}{3} \Rightarrow \dfrac{8}{3} = \dfrac{2x_m + 1}{3} \Rightarrow 2x_m = 7 \Rightarrow x_m = \dfrac{7}{2}$
$y_G = \dfrac{2y_m + y_A}{3} \Rightarrow \dfrac{7}{3} = \dfrac{2y_m + 2}{3} \Rightarrow 2y_m = 5 \Rightarrow y_m = \dfrac{5}{2}$
So, $M \equiv \left(\dfrac{7}{2}, \dfrac{5}{2}\right)$.

Let the vertex $B$ lie on $2x - y = 0$, so its coordinates are $(a, 2a)$.
Let the vertex $C$ lie on $x + y = 3$, so its coordinates are $(b, 3 - b)$.
Since $M$ is the midpoint of $BC$:
$\dfrac{a + b}{2} = \dfrac{7}{2} \Rightarrow a + b = 7$
$\dfrac{2a + 3 - b}{2} = \dfrac{5}{2} \Rightarrow 2a - b = 2$

Adding the two equations:
$3a = 9 \Rightarrow a = 3$
Substituting $a = 3$ into $a + b = 7$ gives $b = 4$.

The coordinates of the vertices are $B(3, 6)$ and $C(4, -1)$.
The equation of the line passing through $B$ and $C$ is:
$y - 6 = \dfrac{-1 - 6}{4 - 3}(x - 3)$
$y - 6 = -7(x - 3)$
$7x + y = 27$

Answer: $7x + y = 27$

6a7a1ff88970af20d7e86166.text: Let $S = \{1, 2, \dots, 20\}$. Let $R_1$ and $R_2$ be relations on $S$ defined as $R_1 = \{(x, y) : x^2 + y^2 \le 200\}$ and $R_2 = \{(x, y) : x \text{ divides } y \text{ and } x \neq y\}$. Then, the number of elements in $R_1 \cap R_2$ is ____.
6a7a1ff88970af20d7e86166.sol:
The relation $R_1 \cap R_2$ contains pairs $(x, y)$ from $S \times S$ such that $x^2 + y^2 \le 200$, $x$ divides $y$, and $x \neq y$.

Since $x$ divides $y$ and $x \neq y$, we can write $y = kx$ for some integer $k \ge 2$. Substituting this into the inequality gives $x^2 + (kx)^2 \le 200$, which simplifies to $x^2(1 + k^2) \le 200$.

We check the possible values of $x \in S$:

For $x = 1$: $1 + y^2 \le 200 \Rightarrow y^2 \le 199$. Since $y \in S$, the maximum value of $y$ is $14$. The possible values for $y$ are multiples of $1$ starting from $2$, so $y \in \{2, 3, \dots, 14\}$. This gives $13$ pairs.

For $x = 2$: $4 + y^2 \le 200 \Rightarrow y^2 \le 196 \Rightarrow y \le 14$. The possible values for $y$ are multiples of $2$ strictly greater than $2$, so $y \in \{4, 6, 8, 10, 12, 14\}$. This gives $6$ pairs.

For $x = 3$: $9 + y^2 \le 200 \Rightarrow y^2 \le 191 \Rightarrow y \le 13$. The possible values for $y$ are multiples of $3$ strictly greater than $3$, so $y \in \{6, 9, 12\}$. This gives $3$ pairs.

For $x = 4$: $16 + y^2 \le 200 \Rightarrow y^2 \le 184 \Rightarrow y \le 13$. The possible values for $y$ are multiples of $4$ strictly greater than $4$, so $y \in \{8, 12\}$. This gives $2$ pairs.

For $x = 5$: $25 + y^2 \le 200 \Rightarrow y^2 \le 175 \Rightarrow y \le 13$. The possible values for $y$ are multiples of $5$ strictly greater than $5$, so $y \in \{10\}$. This gives $1$ pair.

For $x = 6$: $36 + y^2 \le 200 \Rightarrow y^2 \le 164 \Rightarrow y \le 12$. The possible values for $y$ are multiples of $6$ strictly greater than $6$, so $y \in \{12\}$. This gives $1$ pair.

For $x = 7$: $49 + y^2 \le 200 \Rightarrow y^2 \le 151 \Rightarrow y \le 12$. The smallest multiple of $7$ strictly greater than $7$ is $14$, which exceeds $12$. Thus, there are $0$ pairs for $x \ge 7$.

The total number of elements in $R_1 \cap R_2$ is $13 + 6 + 3 + 2 + 1 + 1 = 26$.

Answer: $26$

6a7a1ff8f180ec03c4166feb.text: Let $y = y(x)$ be the solution of the differential equation $\dfrac{dy}{dx} + y \tan x = \dfrac{\sin x \cos x}{1 + \cos^2 x}$ for $x \in \left[0, \dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)$, satisfying $y(0) = -\dfrac{\pi}{4}$. Then the value of the integral $\displaystyle \int_0^{\dfrac{\pi}{2}} y(x) \, dx$ is equal to
6a7a1ff8f180ec03c4166feb.sol:
The given differential equation is a linear differential equation of the form $\dfrac{dy}{dx} + P(x)y = Q(x)$, with $P(x) = \tan x$.

The integrating factor (I.F.) is $e^{\int \tan x \, dx} = e^{\ln(\sec x)} = \sec x$.

The general solution is given by:
$y \sec x = \int \dfrac{\sin x \cos x}{1 + \cos^2 x} \sec x \, dx + C$
$\Rightarrow y \sec x = \int \dfrac{\sin x}{1 + \cos^2 x} \, dx + C$

Let $\cos x = u$, then $-\sin x \, dx = du$.
$\int \dfrac{-du}{1 + u^2} = -\arctan(u) = -\arctan(\cos x)$.
Thus, $y \sec x = -\arctan(\cos x) + C$.

Using the initial condition $y(0) = -\dfrac{\pi}{4}$:
$\left(-\dfrac{\pi}{4}\right) \sec(0) = -\arctan(\cos 0) + C$
$\Rightarrow -\dfrac{\pi}{4} = -\arctan(1) + C \Rightarrow -\dfrac{\pi}{4} = -\dfrac{\pi}{4} + C \Rightarrow C = 0$.

So, $y(x) = -\cos x \arctan(\cos x)$.

We need to evaluate the integral $I = \int_0^{\dfrac{\pi}{2}} y(x) \, dx = \int_0^{\dfrac{\pi}{2}} -\cos x \arctan(\cos x) \, dx$.
Applying integration by parts, let $u = \arctan(\cos x)$ and $dv = -\cos x \, dx$.
Then $du = \dfrac{1}{1 + \cos^2 x}(-\sin x) \, dx$ and $v = -\sin x$.

$I = \left[ -\sin x \arctan(\cos x) \right]_0^{\dfrac{\pi}{2}} - \int_0^{\dfrac{\pi}{2}} \left(-\sin x\right) \left( \dfrac{-\sin x}{1 + \cos^2 x} \right) \, dx$

Evaluating the boundary term:
At $x = \dfrac{\pi}{2}$, $-\sin\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right) \arctan(0) = 0$.
At $x = 0$, $-\sin(0) \arctan(1) = 0$.
So, the boundary term is $0$.

$I = -\int_0^{\dfrac{\pi}{2}} \dfrac{\sin^2 x}{1 + \cos^2 x} \, dx$
$\Rightarrow I = -\int_0^{\dfrac{\pi}{2}} \dfrac{1 - \cos^2 x}{1 + \cos^2 x} \, dx = -\int_0^{\dfrac{\pi}{2}} \left( -1 + \dfrac{2}{1 + \cos^2 x} \right) \, dx$
$\Rightarrow I = \dfrac{\pi}{2} - 2 \int_0^{\dfrac{\pi}{2}} \dfrac{1}{1 + \cos^2 x} \, dx$

To evaluate the remaining integral, divide numerator and denominator by $\cos^2 x$:
$\int_0^{\dfrac{\pi}{2}} \dfrac{\sec^2 x}{\sec^2 x + 1} \, dx = \int_0^{\dfrac{\pi}{2}} \dfrac{\sec^2 x}{2 + \tan^2 x} \, dx$

Let $t = \tan x$, then $dt = \sec^2 x \, dx$. As $x \to \dfrac{\pi}{2}$, $t \to \infty$.
$\int_0^\infty \dfrac{dt}{2 + t^2} = \left[ \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \arctan\left(\dfrac{t}{\sqrt{2}}\right) \right]_0^\infty = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \left( \dfrac{\pi}{2} - 0 \right) = \dfrac{\pi}{2\sqrt{2}}$.

Substituting this back into $I$:
$I = \dfrac{\pi}{2} - 2 \left( \dfrac{\pi}{2\sqrt{2}} \right) = \dfrac{\pi}{2} - \dfrac{\pi}{\sqrt{2}} = \dfrac{\pi}{2}(1 - \sqrt{2})$.

Answer: $\dfrac{\pi}{2}(1 - \sqrt{2})$

6a7a1ff8b6b43e3b645fa7d0.text: Let a point $P$ lie on the line $L_3: \dfrac{x-1}{1} = \dfrac{y+1}{2} = \dfrac{z}{1}$. Let $Q$ be the foot of the perpendicular drawn from $P$ to the plane $\pi: 2x - z = 0$, and $R$ be the foot of the perpendicular drawn from $P$ to the line $L_1: \dfrac{x-1}{1} = \dfrac{y-2}{1} = \dfrac{z-3}{-1}$. If $\angle QPR$ is a right angle, then the square of the distance of $P$ from the origin is ________
6a7a1ff8b6b43e3b645fa7d0.sol:
Let the coordinates of $P$ on the line $L_3$ be $(\lambda + 1, 2\lambda - 1, \lambda)$.

Since $Q$ is the foot of the perpendicular from $P$ to the plane $\pi: 2x - z = 0$, the vector $\vec{PQ}$ is parallel to the normal vector of the plane, $\vec{n} = 2\hat{i} - \hat{k}$.

Let the coordinates of $R$ on the line $L_1$ be $(\mu + 1, \mu + 2, -\mu + 3)$.
The vector $\vec{PR} = (\mu - \lambda)\hat{i} + (\mu - 2\lambda + 3)\hat{j} + (-\mu - \lambda + 3)\hat{k}$.

Since $R$ is the foot of the perpendicular from $P$ to $L_1$, $\vec{PR}$ is perpendicular to the direction of $L_1$ (which is $\hat{i} + \hat{j} - \hat{k}$):
$\vec{PR} \cdot (\hat{i} + \hat{j} - \hat{k}) = 0$
$\Rightarrow 1(\mu - \lambda) + 1(\mu - 2\lambda + 3) - 1(-\mu - \lambda + 3) = 0$
$\Rightarrow \mu - \lambda + \mu - 2\lambda + 3 + \mu + \lambda - 3 = 0$
$\Rightarrow 3\mu - 2\lambda = 0 \Rightarrow \mu = \dfrac{2\lambda}{3}$

We are given that $\angle QPR = 90^{\circ}$, which means $\vec{PQ} \cdot \vec{PR} = 0$.
Since $\vec{PQ}$ is parallel to $\vec{n}$, this implies $\vec{n} \cdot \vec{PR} = 0$:
$(2\hat{i} - \hat{k}) \cdot \vec{PR} = 0$
$\Rightarrow 2(\mu - \lambda) - (-\mu - \lambda + 3) = 0$
$\Rightarrow 2\mu - 2\lambda + \mu + \lambda - 3 = 0$
$\Rightarrow 3\mu - \lambda - 3 = 0$

Substitute $\mu = \dfrac{2\lambda}{3}$ into the equation:
$3\left(\dfrac{2\lambda}{3}\right) - \lambda - 3 = 0$
$\Rightarrow 2\lambda - \lambda - 3 = 0 \Rightarrow \lambda = 3$

Thus, the coordinates of $P$ are $(3 + 1, 2(3) - 1, 3) = (4, 5, 3)$.

The square of the distance of $P$ from the origin is:
$OP^2 = 4^2 + 5^2 + 3^2 = 16 + 25 + 9 = 50$.

Answer: $50$
